title: JASAR v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
summary:
In the case of Jasar v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, the applicant, Mr. Pejrusan Jasar, is a national of the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and a member of the Roma community, represented by lawyers from the European Roma Rights Centre. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police violence and the lack of effective remedies when such abuses occur. On the night of 16 April 1998 in Štip, Mr. Jasar and a Roma friend were present in a bar when a violent incident broke out. Police arrived and, according to Mr. Jasar, subjected him to severe physical abuse both at the scene and later in police custody, resulting in documented injuries. Despite filing a criminal complaint and providing medical evidence, Mr. Jasar’s allegations were not effectively investigated by the authorities, and no charges were brought against him or his friend.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, as well as Article 35 regarding admissibility. The Court found the application admissible, meaning the complaints were sufficiently serious and substantiated to warrant further examination. While the judgment at this stage did not determine a violation, it paved the way for scrutiny of police conduct and state responsibility.

This case is significant as it underscores the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in accessing justice and protection from ill-treatment, reflecting broader patterns of discrimination in Europe’s recent history.
